# Publishing and Proving the Rebuild {#sec-publish}



The guide is finished, and nobody but you can see it: every output sits in a folder on your
computer. This chapter puts it on the web, where anyone can open it on a phone. Then it asks a
question with no prompt attached: one input changes; which outputs change with it, and how do
you know? You will predict first, then rebuild, then check.

::: opener
- Explain what pushing, branches and pull requests add to the commits you already make.
- Make the folder a website and publish it to GitHub Pages.
- Choose between hosts that take your files and hosts that build.
- Predict, rebuild and explain what one changed input reaches.

Start from
: the end of @sec-audiences, with `gh` signed in

You build
: a website, its GitHub repository and the live site

Checkpoint
: none; the catch-up copies `examples/london/`
:::

## Git: every change, safely {#sec-git}

Since the first report (@sec-first-git) you have kept a history yourself: `git status` and
`git diff` before each commit, a message that says why, and `git restore` for a change you did
not want. Publishing needs what Git does beyond the folder: a copy of the history that others
can reach, and a way for someone else to read a change and approve it before it counts.

The vocabulary for that is short (@fig-git-cycle). Your folder is already a *repository*, a
project folder with its history, and each of your commits is a snapshot of every tracked file
with its message. The new words are about sharing them.

![Every change, safely. A team takes each change round the whole loop; working alone, as in this book, you commit to the main line and push.](../media/diagrams/git-cycle){#fig-git-cycle .on-light fig-alt="Six steps. Branch: work on a branch, so main stays untouched. Commit: save a snapshot of the files with a message saying why. Push: copy the commits to GitHub. Pull request: propose the change and show the difference. Review: someone reads the difference and comments, approves or asks for changes. Merge: the commits join main. Working alone, you commit to main and push; in a team, every change goes round the whole loop."}

To *push* is to copy commits to the shared repository on GitHub, the website that keeps a
copy of a repository online. A *branch* is a movable label on a line of commits, so work can go
on there while the main line, `main` (the name `git init -b main` gave it), keeps working. A
*pull request* proposes merging a branch and shows its difference, or *diff*, line by line, as
`git diff` does in your terminal, but on a page that others can read; a *review* comments on
it, approves it or asks for changes; *merging* adds its commits to `main`.

Working alone, as in this book, you commit straight to `main` and push; in a team, every
change goes round the loop. Either way the check is the one you already make: read the diff
before a change counts. From here the agent can run the Git commands too. Ask it to "commit
with a message that says why", and read its diff before you approve: a diff is the clearest
check you have of what the agent actually did.

::: think
The agent reports "Committed the dashboard changes" and asks to push. What do you check
before you approve?

The diff behind the commit: which files and lines changed, that they are the ones you asked
for, that nothing in `data/` or `images/` changed, and that the message says why.
:::

## Where a site lives {#sec-hosting}

A rendered Quarto website is *static*: a folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and documents,
with no program running on a server. Any web server can serve it, so publishing means copying
that folder to a host. **GitHub Pages** is the host this book uses: GitHub keeps a copy of the
history you have been committing, GitHub Pages serves the site from it, and
`quarto publish gh-pages` is built in (@fig-publish-flow).

![Publishing to GitHub Pages. The source goes to the `main` branch with Git; `quarto publish gh-pages` renders the site on your computer and pushes only the rendered HTML to a separate branch, which GitHub serves.](../media/diagrams/publish-flow){#fig-publish-flow .on-light fig-alt="Your project folder holds the source, which git pushes to the main branch of a GitHub repository. quarto publish gh-pages renders the site on your computer and pushes only the rendered HTML to a separate branch, gh-pages. GitHub Pages serves that branch at https://user.github.io/repo/. Anyone with the address can read the site."}

There are two ways to get a site onto a host. Either you render on your own computer and
upload the result, as `quarto publish` does for GitHub Pages and Netlify, or the host builds
the site from your repository on every push, in a *CI job*, a build it runs for you. The
second works only if the build installs
Quarto, Python and every package the project needs, or if the rendered output is committed.
The London repository leaves its rendered `_site/` folder out, so a host that builds would
produce nothing until the build is set up.

::: think
You connect `london-guide` to a host that builds from Git, and it publishes an empty site. Why?

The repository holds no rendered site, because `.gitignore` leaves `_site/` out, and the host's
build has no Quarto, Python or packages unless you install them in it. Either render on your
computer and upload the result, or set up the build.
:::

@tbl-hosts sorts the hosts by route. Their free plans change, so @tbl-hosts-free in
@sec-facts lists each one's current limits, and Cloudflare's, with the date they were checked:
read them before choosing.

| Host | How the site gets there |
|---|---|
| [GitHub Pages](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html) | `quarto publish gh-pages` renders and uploads it: this book's route |
| [Netlify](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/netlify.html) | `quarto publish netlify` renders and uploads it |
| a host that builds: [Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/plans/hobby), [GitLab Pages](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/pages/), [Render](https://render.com/docs/static-sites) | it builds the site from the repository on every push |

: Three routes onto a host. {#tbl-hosts}

Quarto's Netlify build plugin runs no Python, so for this project, render and upload.

## One folder, one website {#sec-london-website}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Make this folder a Quarto website: _quarto.yml (render only the .qmd files; navbar: Guide, Dashboard, a Downloads menu for the docx, pdf, pptx, epub and london-slides.html files that exist) and index.qmd, and add /_site/ to .gitignore. Render and check the links.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes 2 files · adds a line to `.gitignore` · `uv run quarto render` → `_site/`
:::

::: {.you}
then, in the preview tab: Ctrl+C, and `uv run quarto preview`
:::

A `_quarto.yml` file at the top of the folder turns it into a *project*. `quarto render` with no
file name then builds every listed page into `_site/`, with shared navigation, and `quarto
preview` with no file name previews the whole site. The dashboard becomes one page of it:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  render:                       # <1>
    - index.qmd
    - london.qmd
    - london-dashboard.qmd
website:
  title: "Visit London"
  navbar:
    left:
      - {text: Guide, href: london.qmd}
      - {text: Dashboard, href: london-dashboard.qmd}
      - {text: Downloads, menu: [...]}    # <2>
```
1. An explicit `render` list keeps the README, the data notes and the photo credits from
   becoming pages of the site.
2. The menu links the files the other formats wrote: the Word guide, the PDF, the flyer, and
   whichever optional files you made.

`.gitignore` gains one line, for the rendered site, `_site/`, which is rebuilt from the source
and published separately (@sec-london-publish). The rest of the list has been there since you
started the folder (@sec-brief): the environment `.venv/` (rebuilt from `uv.lock`), Quarto's
working files and the outputs rendered beside the sources. `index.qmd` becomes the site's
home page, `index.html`, the page a visitor sees at the site's address.

::: tryit
Make the folder a website and restart the preview.

::: done
the site opens with Guide, Dashboard and Downloads in its navigation bar, and each Downloads
link opens its file.
:::
:::

## Publish {#sec-london-publish}

Publishing takes two prompts and one command of your own. Before you paste the prompts,
replace `<your-github-username>` in them with your GitHub username (the agent can look it up
with `gh api user` if you ask it to). The first readies the folder:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Check that .gitignore covers _site/, .quarto/, .venv/, *_files/, *.quarto_ipynb, london*.html, *.docx, *.pdf, *.pptx and *.epub. Replace README.md with a short one linking to https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/ and listing the files in the site's Downloads menu. Commit it with any work not yet committed. Show me the README and `git status`.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
reads `.gitignore` · writes `README.md` · `git add` · `git commit` · `git status`
:::

::: {.you}
approve its commands · read the README · check that `git status` says `nothing to commit, working tree clean`
:::

The second puts the folder on GitHub:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create a public GitHub repository named `london-guide` with gh and push `main` to it. Set the repository's website to https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/ with `gh repo edit --homepage`. Show me the repository's URL and the website URL you set.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`gh repo create london-guide …` · `gh repo edit --homepage …`
:::

::: {.you}
approve `gh` · in the preview tab: Ctrl+C, then `uv run quarto publish gh-pages` and Enter · open the address on your phone
:::

The agent creates the repository on GitHub from your folder with `gh repo create
london-guide --public --source=. --push`, which also pushes the commits, using the sign-in
from the setup check. Every commit you have made since you started the folder goes with them,
so the repository on GitHub opens with the guide's whole history, one checked step at a
time. Its README is the first thing visitors to the repository
see, and its link takes them on to the live site.

<!-- Quarto's GitHub Pages guide, https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html, read
2026-11-25: "Before configuring the publishing action, it's important that you run quarto
publish gh-pages locally, once." The publish "will confirm that you want to publish, render
your content, copy the output to a special gh-pages branch, push that branch to GitHub, and
then open a browser". In the workshop's earlier dry run, the first publish of each site took
one and a half to two minutes, and GitHub Pages then built it in 20 to 35 seconds. -->

The first publish is yours, typed in the terminal, because Quarto's GitHub Pages guide asks
for one local `quarto publish gh-pages` before any automated one. Stop the preview first: the
publish renders the whole site, and two renders in one folder collide. It asks one question,
"Publish site … (Y/n)", which Enter answers yes; then it renders the site, creates the
`gh-pages` branch, pushes the rendered site and opens it. A 404 page in the first minute
usually means the site is still being deployed. Once the branch exists, the agent can update
the site with `uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt`.

::: pitfall
A push that fails with `HTTP 400` ("RPC failed", "the remote end hung up unexpectedly") was seen
with larger sites, such as dashboards with embedded maps. Raise Git's buffer for this repository
with `git config http.postBuffer 524288000`, and push again.
:::

::: practice
Publishing from your own computer is simple and keeps the build where your environment is. The
alternative, a GitHub Action that renders on every push (Quarto's
`quarto-dev/quarto-actions`), needs Python and the project's packages installed in the job,
or `freeze` set so that committed results are reused, and Quarto's guide still asks for one
local `quarto publish gh-pages` first.
:::

::: tryit
Publish the guide.

::: done
`https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/london-dashboard.html` opens on your
phone.
:::

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/README.md
```
:::

## Change one input, explain the rebuild {#sec-london-change}

@sec-drift listed what goes wrong when a correction has to be carried by hand into every file
that quotes it. Here is the correction for real, in a project where no visitor count was ever
copied. You made the
same move on a smaller scale with the first report (@sec-first-change) and predicted one for
the guide's first three formats (@sec-formats); now it covers every page. No prompt is
supplied: write your own, or do it by hand. Make the edit to the data yourself, for example
with `nano data/attractions.csv` (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X): the project's rules keep the
agent out of `data/`, which is the point of them.

::: tryit
1. **Predict.** Set the Tower's `visits_2025` to `8000000`. Which outputs will change? Write
   it down.
2. **Rebuild**: stop the preview, `uv run quarto render`.
3. **Explain** what changed and what did not.
4. **Undo**: `git restore data/attractions.csv`, rebuild.

::: done
you can name what changed, what did not, and the line of code that links each changed output
to the input.
:::
:::

The value is fictitious: chosen to change the top attraction, so that the effect is visible,
and reversible, because the real file has been committed since you copied it in
(@sec-md-table). `git restore` puts a file
back as it was at the last commit, and the second rebuild leaves no trial number in your files.

### Check your prediction {.unnumbered}

To check, you need to know which page reads which input. @tbl-london-deps is computed from the
finished project's sources, optional pages included: a page counts as reading a file only if its
code loads it.

::: {#tbl-london-deps .cell tbl-cap='Which page of the finished London project (each a `.qmd` file) reads which file in `data/`. Computed from the sources: a mark means the page\'s code loads the file.' execution_count=2}
| Page | attrac­tions | visits | churches | sights |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| london | ● |  |  |  |
| london-dashboard | ● | ● | ● |  |
| london-email | ● |  |  |  |
| london-flyer |  |  |  |  |
| london-social | ● |  |  |  |
| london-whitepaper | ● | ● |  |  |
:::




The guide writes six files, as html\, docx\, pdf\, pptx\, epub and slides;
every other page writes one. In all, five pages load
`attractions.csv`, and between them they write ten files, so the
change reaches all of them at the next render.

What it does there depends on each page's code. Of those pages, three
(the guide, the dashboard and the partner brief) find the top attraction with
`attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()` and the total with `.sum()`, so in each of them the Tower
of London becomes the most visited attraction and the total rises. The square advert uses only
the first call, so it names the Tower too.

The white paper names no top attraction: its sums by
admission change, but its table keeps ALVA's `rank_uk` column from the file, which would still
rank the Tower ninth in the UK beside the most visits of the ten. A
copied column goes stale too. Still, the correction reaches ten
files with one command, and nobody has to go looking for them.

Copies deserve a second look. The flyer loads no data at all, and the sights tables in the
guide and the partner brief are typed, although the guide's credits name `sights.csv`: all
three *copy* their facts (price bands, nearest stations) from the cited file into the
Markdown. That was a reasonable choice, because those facts rarely change, but it means a
correction to `sights.csv` updates none of them. A cited copy is still a copy.

::: why
Why does every page recompute, even ones whose sources did not change? The project keeps
Quarto's default, `freeze: false`, so every render re-runs every page's code; with caching on,
a page whose own source did not change would keep its old numbers (@sec-publish-many).
:::

Two more things do not change: the live site, until you publish again
(`uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt`), and any output you did not rebuild. Model
answers, with the follow-up questions worth asking, are in @sec-checkpoints.

## A white paper (optional) {#sec-london-whitepaper}

The same data can also become an academic paper: an abstract, numbered sections, computed results
and a reference list, set in the typeface LaTeX documents use, without installing LaTeX.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create london-whitepaper.qmd, an A4 Typst white paper in "New Computer Modern": an abstract (no inline code), numbered Introduction, Methods, Results and Conclusions, then References via `#set bibliography(title: [References])` (references.bib from `url`). Analyse data/visits.csv vs 2019 and data/attractions.csv by `admission`. Add it to `render` and the "Downloads" menu; render; check citations. Figures must be vector: set `fig-format: svg` and check that the files in `figure-typst/` end in .svg.
```
:::

```yaml
bibliography: references.bib
format:
  typst:
    mainfont: "New Computer Modern"    # <1>
    section-numbering: "1.1"           # <2>
    bibliographystyle: ieee            # <3>
    fig-format: svg                    # <4>
```
1. Typst 0.15, bundled with Quarto 1.10.20, includes New Computer Modern, the OpenType version of
   LaTeX's Computer Modern, so the paper looks like a LaTeX article without a TeX installation.
2. Numbers the headings: 1, 1.1, 2.
3. Typst's numbered reference style; `[@key]` in the text cites an entry in `references.bib`.
4. Vector figures stay sharp at any zoom; the prompt's check makes sure they really are vectors.

![Page 1 of the finished London white paper.](../media/figures/london-whitepaper-p1.png){#fig-whitepaper width=75% .on-light fig-alt="The first page of an A4 paper set in a LaTeX-style typeface: the title Visits to London's leading ALVA member attractions, 2015 to 2025, the subtitle Pandemic loss and recovery: a descriptive analysis, the author London Tourism Office, an abstract, and sections 1, Introduction, and 2, Methods, with numbered citations in square brackets."}

The paper's settings need Quarto 1.10 or newer. Two more traps were met while building the
example (@tbl-whitepaper-traps).

| You see | Because | Do |
|---|---|---|
| inline code in the YAML `abstract` fails | it runs before the setup cell | write the abstract in the body, in a raw Typst block |
| a "Bibliography" heading over the references | Typst prints its own heading there | `#set bibliography(title: [References])`, and no heading of your own |

: Two traps met while building the white paper. {#tbl-whitepaper-traps}

A genuine LaTeX PDF is also available, as `format: pdf`, but it needs a TeX distribution, for
example `quarto install tinytex`. For most reports Typst is faster and simpler.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- Pushing copies your commits to GitHub; a pull request shows a diff for someone else to
  review before it counts.
- A built site is static files: upload them, or let a host build them.
- A `_quarto.yml` with a render list makes a folder a website.
- The first `quarto publish gh-pages` is yours; later updates can be the agent's.
- A changed input reaches every page whose code loads it; copies and the live site do not.
:::

That completes one guide for many audiences. The exercises that follow leave the prompts out,
and hide one stale number for you to find. After them, Part III takes one set of results to
the documents a company is asked for: a model card, a deck, a site and a white paper.
